# How keeping active pays off in the olfactory system

## Authors

- Kevin Monahan<sup>1</sup>
- Stavros Lomvardas<sup>2</sup> †

### Affiliations

1. Department of Anatomy University of California San Francisco USA
2. Department of Anatomy University of California San Francisco USA stavros.lomvardas@ucsf.edu

† Corresponding author

## Abstract

A protein that is found in the main olfactory epithelium of mice ensures that odour-sensing neurons that are active to have longer lifespans than those that are inactive.

claims.claim: A protein found in the main olfactory epithelium of mice ensures that odour-sensing neurons that are active have longer lifespans than those that are inactive.
claims.source_text: A protein that is found in the main olfactory epithelium of mice ensures that odour-sensing neurons that are active to have longer lifespans than those that are inactive.
claims.evidence_reasoning: This claim is stated in the abstract as a summary of findings, but no experimental data, measurements, or citations are provided in the manuscript excerpt to support it. It appears to be an inference about the content of the full paper.

claims.claim: Neuronal activity influences lifespan of odour-sensing neurons in the main olfactory epithelium.
claims.source_text: A protein that is found in the main olfactory epithelium of mice ensures that odour-sensing neurons that are active to have longer lifespans than those that are inactive.
claims.evidence_reasoning: This claim is logically inferred from the statement that active neurons have longer lifespans than inactive ones, implying that activity level is a determinant of neuronal lifespan.

claims.claim: There is a differential survival mechanism between active and inactive odour-sensing neurons in mice.
claims.source_text: A protein that is found in the main olfactory epithelium of mice ensures that odour-sensing neurons that are active to have longer lifespans than those that are inactive.
claims.evidence_reasoning: The existence of different lifespans based on activity status implies a mechanism that differentially affects survival of these neuron populations, though the specific mechanism is not detailed in this excerpt.

claims.claim: A specific protein mediates the relationship between neuronal activity and lifespan in olfactory neurons.
claims.source_text: A protein that is found in the main olfactory epithelium of mice ensures that odour-sensing neurons that are active to have longer lifespans than those that are inactive.
claims.evidence_reasoning: The abstract explicitly states that 'a protein' ensures the lifespan difference, indicating protein-mediated regulation, though no experimental evidence is provided in this excerpt.

results.result: The authors report that a protein in the main olfactory epithelium of mice mediates activity-dependent neuronal survival, where active odour-sensing neurons have longer lifespans than inactive ones. This implies a differential survival mechanism regulated by neuronal activity through protein-mediated pathways.
results.result_reasoning: All claims (C1-C4) are based solely on the abstract statement with no experimental data, statistical analysis, controls, or methodological details provided in the manuscript excerpt. The identity of the protein, the experimental approach to measure neuronal lifespan, methods to distinguish active from inactive neurons, sample sizes, and statistical significance are all absent. Without access to the experimental evidence, it is impossible to evaluate whether the claims are supported by rigorous data or appropriate controls.
